lmsArticle.title: System Design HLD Example: Web Crawler
lmsArticle.subtitle: A practical interview-ready HLD for a distributed web crawler handling politeness, deduplication, and scale.
lmsArticle.excerpt: A distributed web crawler must balance global throughput with per-domain politeness. The architectural crux is the **URL Frontier**, which manages priority and rate-limiting across a distributed fetcher pool. By combining **Bloom Filters** for URL deduplication and **SimHash** for content near-duplicate detection, the system can crawl billions of pages while maintaining a minimal storage footprint and respecting the stability of the target websites.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

A distributed web crawler must balance global throughput with per-domain politeness. The architectural crux is the **URL Frontier**, which manages priority and rate-limiting across a distributed fetcher pool. By combining **Bloom Filters** for URL deduplication and **SimHash** for content near-duplicate detection, the system can crawl billions of pages while maintaining a minimal storage footprint and respecting the…

This walkthrough focuses on **How Googlebot, Bingbot, and CommonCrawl Deploy Crawler Architecture at Scale**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Googlebot indexes over 130 trillion web pages and is the world's most sophisticated crawler.
- Google's published patents and engineering papers describe a URL Frontier nearly identical to the two-queue architecture above, augmented with a "freshness" layer that dynamically adjusts re-crawl frequency based on obs…
- News sites are re-crawled hourly, product listing pages daily, and static documentation monthly.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, stack-and-queue-data-structures, caching, hash-tables-and-bloom-filters

## Stage 1 — URL Deduplication Strategy Decision Framework

-

**Observable outcome:** You can explain how “URL Deduplication Strategy Decision Framework” changes the architecture or implementation path.

## Stage 2 — Presenting the Web Crawler HLD in a System Design Interview

- Start every web crawler answer by drawing the core loop on the whiteboard: Frontier → Fetcher → Content Store → Link Extractor → Frontier.
- This loop is the entire system.
- Every other component — Bloom Filter, SimHash Engine, Robots.txt cache, DNS cache — is a correctness or performance guard on one of the loop's stages.
- Interviewers reliably probe three specific areas in every web crawler question.

*Applies **stack-and-queue-data-structures** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Presenting the Web Crawler HLD in a System Design Interview - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant",
    "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** Interviewers reliably probe three specific areas in every web crawler question.

## Stage 3 — What Building a Web Crawler Teaches About Adversarial Distributed Systems

- A web crawler is a distributed system that must cooperate with millions of external systems — the web's servers — over which it has zero control.
- This forces architectural decisions that most internal distributed systems never encounter: adversarial environments, unpredictable response times, resource-constrained counterparties, and legal constraints from robots.…
- Every design choice in a web crawler is a negotiation between the crawler's appetite for throughput and the web's need for stability.
- The politeness constraint is not merely an ethical guideline — it is a self-preservation mechanism.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The politeness constraint is not merely an ethical guideline — it is a self-preservation mechanism.

## End-to-end outcome

Googlebot indexes over 130 trillion web pages and is the world's most sophisticated crawler.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### The Core Trade-offs in Web Crawler Architecture

- **Detection:** Breadth-First Traversal: A depth-first crawler follows the first link on every page as deep as possible before backtracking.
- **User or operator impact:** Breadth-First Traversal: A depth-first crawler follows the first link on every page as deep as possible before backtracking.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
